title: Word Frequency With operator[]
statement:
`std::map<std::string, int>`'s `operator[]` has a property worth knowing
cold: asking for a key that is not there yet does not fail or read
garbage -- it **inserts that key with a value-initialised value** (`0` for
`int`) and returns a reference to it. That is a genuinely different
contract from some other languages' map/dictionary types, and it is
exactly the behaviour a frequency counter wants.

## Your function

```
std::map<std::string, int> WordFrequency(const std::string& text);
```

Return a map from each distinct whitespace-separated word in `text` to how
many times it occurs. `text` may be empty, in which case the result is an
empty map. Matching is case-sensitive: `"Cat"` and `"cat"` are different
words.

## Watch out

- **`counts[word]++` is not a bug here the way it would be in some other
  languages -- it is the whole function.** The first time `word` is seen,
  `counts[word]` creates the entry as `0` and hands back a reference to
  it, which `++` then turns into `1`; every later occurrence reads the
  entry that is already there and increments it further. One line, no
  branch, correct on the first occurrence and every one after.
- **Matching is case-sensitive on purpose.** `"Cat"` and `"cat"` are
  different keys in the map -- do not lower-case anything before counting.
- **`std::map` keeps its keys in sorted order** (unlike
  `std::unordered_map`), which is exactly why the harness below can print
  every word and count by walking the map directly and get a predictable
  order back -- nothing about *this* function has to sort anything itself.

tests.name: an empty line has no words
every word distinct -- the case a bare counts[word]++ handles on its own
case-sensitive: Cat and cat are different keys
tests.description: Three distinct keys by exact case, sorted lexicographically by std::map -- capitals sort before lower case in ASCII.

tests.name: words printed in sorted key order
